7.0.s.en: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

7.0.0.en: In this chapter, since it was difficult for the Jews, who had lived many years keeping the traditions of the Law, to give it up suddenly after the resurrection of Christ, St. Paul began to prove that the Law with its ordinances no longer has dominion over man. He addressed his words to the Jews who knew the Law, expressing astonishment that they had forgotten and been ignorant of the fact that the Law is laid down only for the living, meaning that a person is obliged to carry out the rites of the law of Moses only as long as he is alive, since death nullifies any contract between two parties.

7.1.0.en: St. Paul gave an example of this, which is the woman's obligation to the law (the statute) that binds her to her husband as long as he lives; she cannot leave him and marry another man unless her husband dies, and then she is free from the law that regulates her marital relationship with that man.

7.2.0.en: The woman, during her husband's life, cannot be joined to another man or she would be called an adulteress, but if he dies she can be joined to another man and in this case is not called an adulteress.

7.3.0.en: So you also, Christians of Jewish origin: the Law regulated the relationship between you and the old man, that is, your nature inclined to evil, just as the law binds the woman, who signifies your souls, and the man, who signifies the old man.

7.3.1.en: The Law and the commandments are like the bridle that restrains your instincts and abilities, so that they do not swerve after the old man, who is inclined to evil. And when the old man died with Christ on the Cross, the soul was freed from the dominion of the old man over it and from the Law, and became free to be joined to another, who is the new Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ, with His new statutes and laws for it in the New Testament. The fruit of this marital union is the fruits of the Holy Spirit and good works.

7.4.0.en: The flesh: that is, that in which the old man works, namely the nature inclined to evil. By the law: by which the Law shows its ugliness and evil.

7.4.1.en: In the Old Testament, when people lived in the flesh inclined to evil, the evil passions, whose ugliness the Law shows, worked in man. And so his fate was death and going down to Hades.

7.5.0.en: Wherein we were held: united with it in our body.

7.5.1.en: Now, after the completion of redemption and the death of the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil that worked in the man in whom we were held, we were freed from him and from the Law that governed our relationship with him, and we were joined to Christ, and we have a new relationship with Him regulated by a new rule, which is the worship of God in the Spirit, and not the formal relationship of the literal application of the Law.

7.5.2.en: Do you gladden God's heart by rising from formal worship of the flesh to the release of the spirit and its soaring in heavenly things in a relationship of mutual love with God? Then your fasting becomes not only of the body, but you rise above material things and outward shows that magnify living, so that your prostration with the body is in humility and contrition in spirit, and your prayer is deep and burning with love for your heavenly Bridegroom.

7.6.s.en: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

7.6.0.en: The matter became confused for some people, who thought that the Law and sin are one thing, on the grounds that we were freed from both at the same time after Christ. Certainly the Law is not sin; God forbid that this be true. The Law made known to me sins of all kinds and forms, but it forbade me from them. The Law said to me, "Thou shalt not covet," and instead of keeping away from desire and rejoicing in God's commandment, I desired sin more, acting on the psychological principle that says (the forbidden is desired).

7.7.0.en: The commandment revealed sin, and the soul clung to it instead of leaving it; that is, the commandment revealed evil to me, so I sought it and clung to it. And the phrase "without the law sin was dead" does not mean that sin did not exist, but the meaning is that before the Law man committed sin as something natural in his daily conduct, not knowing that this conduct was sin; that is, he thought sin did not exist, as though it were dead, and then the Law came and revealed his sins.

7.7.1.en: Man's failure to recognize sin before the Law was because man had warped the conscience by which he distinguished wrong from right, so he needed the Law to guide him and reveal sin to him.

7.8.0.en: St. Paul confirmed his words by saying that before the Law man practiced sin as an ordinary thing, killing, cursing, stealing, and getting angry, and he lived in the flesh, that is, he lived a fleshly, animal, unspiritual life and was content with his state. The law of Moses had not yet come to reveal his sins and count them against him, but when the commandment came with the Law, man realized his predicament and said to himself, "I am surely lost and I shall die because of my sins."

7.8.1.en: And the phrase "sin revived" does not mean that it was dead and then lived, but the meaning is that man was able to recognize it through the Law, so it was revealed and became alive, and at the same time man's fault and his deserving of death appeared.

7.9.0.en: The commandment, which was supposed to rescue man from a life of sin to a life of holiness, stood only as a dry statute, since the Law did not stretch out its hand to help man to be delivered from sin, being content only with holding him accountable and then sentencing him to death.

7.10.0.en: The commandment made me know sin, so Satan intervened to make sin attractive to me, and sin deceived me, as I thought it would satisfy my needs and make my life easy, so I fell into it and was sentenced to death; that is, sin slew me.

7.11.0.en: The Law is holy, just, and good because it is words that came out of the mouth of the holy God, and the wise man loves the Law, understands it, and applies it, but the fool who twists the commandments to suit his desire deceives himself and falls into sin and death.

7.12.0.en: The Law cannot be blamed as the cause of the fool's conduct in evil and then his death, just as a judge cannot be blamed and described as a murderer if he sentences a criminal to death. Consequently, the goodness of the Law cannot become a cause of death except for one who wanted for himself disobedience to the Law and twisting its commandments. How cunning is Satan! He incites to the doing of sin, exploiting every opportunity to make man fall, and he was not content with that, but exploited even God's commandments to make propaganda for sin and make it known to people. Thus sin becomes something hateful and exceedingly sinful, because it was not ashamed of God's commandment but rather exploited it for its own benefit.

7.12.1.en: Perhaps you, my friend, have now realized that Satan wants to seduce you into sin even by exploiting the commandment itself. Therefore read and understand your Holy Bible well, going deeply into it with care, for how many people perished when they misunderstood some verses or interpreted them in a way that matched their personal desire, or adopted the principle of the single verse without trying to know the circumstances of the writing of each verse, how and to whom it was said, and without even comparing it with the rest of the texts of Scripture. And if you are a servant, or a father or a mother, do not speak in detail about sins lest you stir the senses of the one you serve, and do not speak about new kinds of sins lest you arouse the curiosity of the one you serve, so that he goes after these new sins to discover and practice them.

7.13.s.en: (3) The conflict between the good will and the sin dwelling in

7.13.0.en: Here St. Paul begins, with wonderful eloquence, to describe the inner psychological conflict of the man who loves good but is overcome by evil, starting by declaring that he respects the Law and does not diminish its worth, since the Law is spiritual, delivered by the disposition of angels (Acts 7:53), and he casts all the causes of sin upon himself as a man of flesh and blood before his union with the Holy Spirit. So St. Paul says on behalf of every soul: I am a man "sold under sin" like a slave in the captivity of sin; the spiritual law demands that I follow goodness without help, and the result is that I am a man torn between the demands of the spirit and the reality of the flesh enslaved to sin.

7.14.0.en: I, as a man, do not understand this strange contradiction between my will and my conduct, for my will hates evil but I am overcome by it and weak before it, and the result is that I sin despite the cry of my conscience. For example, I want not to be angry, because anger causes many problems, but when I am provoked I fall into it. So I did not do what I want (longsuffering), but I did what I do not want, which is anger.

7.15.0.en: Since I do sin while in my inner self I do not want it, then I am at heart a friend of the Law; I love it and bear witness within me that it is good, because it rejects sin as I reject it.

7.16.0.en: Sin that dwells in me: the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil that is within me. Who then does the sin, if I do not want to do it? It is the nature inclined to evil dwelling in me, that is, the old man.

7.17.0.en: Dwelleth in me: my nature inclined to evil.

7.17.1.en: I find not: I cannot do good because of my nature's inclination to evil.

7.17.2.en: The Apostle affirms the inclination of human nature to evil before the work of the grace of Christ in the New Testament, in the sacrament of Baptism and the rest of the sacraments. Although man's will, moved by conscience and the commandments of the Law, wants to do good, it cannot keep away from evil because of man's weak resistance to sin; rather, he inclines to it easily.

7.18.0.en: The final result is that I cannot do the good that my good will seeks, but I do evil because my nature is inclined to it. The good will is a mere desire that no power for carrying out supports, while all the inclinations of my nature go toward evil.

7.19.0.en: This is a confirmation of the previous verse, that the evil I do results from my nature inclined to it, against my good will, which is weak and unable to carry out the good.

7.20.0.en: Sadly, the increase of man's knowledge of goodness through the Law is matched, on the other hand, by an intensity of submission to evil, and in this he tears apart the human soul.

7.21.0.en: The inward man: the conscience of man, which moves his mind and heart to good, and is therefore in agreement with the good commandments of the Law.

7.22.0.en: There is another law, which is the law of sin, that is, my evil desires to carry out sin without limits, which compels me to commit sin although the law of my mind, that is, my conscience, rejects this sin.

7.23.0.en: Who will deliver me, the wretched man, after I have been unable to resist? My will is weak and powerless; it cannot give me victory over my body and my human thought, which wanted sin and did it, so that it became a body condemned to death. And the question received its answer: the Deliverer is Christ, by His saving grace through Baptism and the sacraments of the Church and all the means of grace.

7.24.0.en: St. Paul thanks God on my behalf and yours, since the Deliverer and Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, has come to end the conflict and break the chains of sins, release the captives, and reconcile the inward man with the body, so that man is reconciled with God.

7.24.1.en: St. Paul also thanks God because the law of sin was in force over his body only and not over his mind, which served the law of God. In this his state was better than that of the Gentiles, who served the law of sin with the body and the mind also, so they walked in evil because the commandments of the Law did not warn them and they had only the conscience, which is easily warped and turned aside.

7.24.2.en: As for Paul, the problem of the law of sin dwelling in his body was solved when he received the sacrament of Baptism, so the old man died and he became, in mind and body, a servant of the laws and commandments of Christ. In this he received complete justification and became not liable to judgment, and the tears of repentance became a second baptism for him at any time he falls into sin, and then rises and declares his refusal to submit to it.

7.24.3.en: If you enjoy the grace of Christ which gives you strength to walk in the good way, do not give opportunity to the evil that dominates you, by keeping away from the sources of sin and drawing near to the Church, so that your strength increases. And do not be troubled by your many falls, for the grace of Christ to which you cling is able in the end to overcome every weakness or evil inclination that is generated within you as a result of your occasional negligence. Only persevere in repentance and in asking God's help.

7.24.4.en: The good pleasure of the loving Christ orders our life and gives us eternity

8.0.s.en: (1) No condemnation to those who walk after the Spirit

8.0.0.en: Here we have reached with St. Paul the Holy of Holies of the Epistle, which is that those united with Christ Jesus have been rescued from judgment and the door of Paradise has finally been opened to them, on condition that they walk in a spiritual walk, subject to the commandments of Christ and not led after fleshly passions and desires.

8.1.0.en: The law of the Spirit of life: the commandments of the New Testament supported by the power of the Holy Spirit.

8.1.1.en: The law of sin and death: the nature inclined to evil, which leads to man's destruction. Why is there no condemnation on the children of the New Testament?

8.1.2.en: Because the new spiritual law leading to eternal life has freed those united with Christ from the dominion of sin, that is, its law over them, and consequently freed them from death as the wages of sin. And how is that?

8.1.3.en: Through Christ, who was not content with commandments and teachings, but gave them the Holy Spirit, by whom they are able to carry out those commandments and overcome sin.

8.1.4.en: Note, beloved, that St. Paul mentioned the word Spirit in this chapter 20 times, in contrast to his mention of the word I, the defeated one, 20 times in the previous chapter, to highlight the helplessness of the I in contrast to victory by the Spirit in this chapter.

8.2.0.en: It was weak: unable to support man in carrying out the commandment.

8.2.1.en: Weak through the flesh: the flesh weak before sin and inclined to it.

8.2.2.en: In the likeness of sinful flesh: Christ became incarnate in a complete human body but not inclined to sin, so he calls it "likeness" because it is pure and not inclined to sin.

8.2.3.en: For sin: to overcome sin and not fall into it.

8.2.4.en: Condemned sin: He showed its evil, for it had enslaved man throughout the Old Testament, but now, through the incarnation of Christ, man receives the new nature in the sacrament of Baptism, so he inclines to good and rejects evil. The Law showed goodness, but it was unable to help the flesh inclined to evil, so man was doing evil. But when Christ became incarnate to free us from sin, He gave us a new nature inclined to good, so He showed the error and evil of sin, and man no longer wants it as long as he is attached to God.

8.3.0.en: In this we are able to fulfill the righteousness of the Law, so we are righteous in the Law's sight and it has nothing to complain of against us, because we have become walkers and led by the Spirit of God in a spiritual life. Note, beloved, that there is no contradiction between the commandments of the law of Moses and the commandments of Christ, as the Lord Christ Himself said, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil" (Mt 5:17).

8.4.0.en: Those who are still under the dominion of the flesh, we find all their concerns and conversations confined to fleshly matters: what shall we eat, what shall we drink, what shall we wear, or what shall we enjoy? You find no place for spiritual matters in their lives. They are in the flesh and live for the flesh.

8.4.1.en: But the spiritual person who loves God and makes pleasing Him his first goal is concerned with spiritual things such as prayer, spiritual readings, fasts, and Liturgies, and you find his bodily concerns reasonable, balanced, and disciplined, that is, governed by the Spirit.

8.5.0.en: The flesh is not evil in itself, but concern with and indulgence in fleshly desires is the error that leads to spiritual death and separation from God. As for the spiritual person, his heart is filled with peace, and his soul lives from the death of sin.

8.6.0.en: What the flesh asks is opposed to what the Spirit asks, and the principle St. Paul lays down here is clear: whoever has focused all his concerns on his body has left God's sphere for the sphere of the world hostile to God, and cannot submit to the law of God even if he wants to, because his pampered body draws him to various desires, preventing him from carrying out the commandments pleasing to God. How can a slack body keep watch in prayer, how can a body stuffed with food fast, how can a swollen ego be humble, and how can the fornicator live a life of holiness?

8.7.0.en: But if the Spirit of God dwells and lives in us, we are not called fleshly but spiritual, living in the world while it does not live in us, as though we were visitors, strangers to it, using from the world only what is necessary for our life with contentment and satisfaction, without greed or magnifying of living.

8.7.1.en: So all these preceding verses show that Baptism alone is not enough for our salvation unless we practice a life worthy of this gift after receiving it. And the one who has no love and conviction for the way of Christ, and is not submissive to the Holy Spirit, hindering His work, as though he did not have the Spirit of Christ within him, this one has no peace and will not have eternal life.

8.8.0.en: If we walk by the Spirit and are united with Christ, then at the end of our life on earth the body will submit to natural death as a result of the original sin, while the spirit will have eternal life because of the life of righteousness we lived with the support of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us. Likewise, when Christ is united with us, the body dies to sin, that is, it rejects it and is repelled by it, while the spirit in which Christ works lives to righteousness by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

8.9.0.en: The Spirit of Him that raised up Jesus: the Holy Spirit, who raised Christ: God the Father.

8.9.1.en: Shall also quicken your mortal bodies: although the body must die, it will rise on the last day in a new spiritual form, united with the spirit to be glorified with it.

8.9.2.en: His Spirit that dwelleth in you: the Holy Spirit.

8.9.3.en: So God is able to raise our bodies on the last day, that both the body and the spirit (the risen spiritual body) may enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven with Christ.

8.9.4.en: This verse also gives hope to every soul, that Christ is able to raise it from the falls of sin however hideous, if it wants repentance and insists on striving.

8.10.0.en: After all the preceding free gifts of God, we are debtors to Him for our lives and our spirits, and it is not right for us to live as slaves of the flesh and its desires, as though we were debtors to the flesh for anything.

8.11.0.en: For if we live doing the works of the flesh, which are evil desires (Gal 5:19, 20), the result is eternal death. But if we resist the works of the flesh by spiritual fullness, we can easily overcome, and then we enjoy eternal bliss with Christ.

8.12.0.en: Are led: accept God's arrangements in their lives.

8.12.1.en: Here the Apostle shows the depth of the spiritual life with God. The person who confidently surrenders his life to God's leading, accepting from Him all the events of his life, thanking Him for the sweet ones and being patient in the bitter ones, this one is called a son of God.

8.13.0.en: Abba: a Syriac word meaning father.

8.13.1.en: Father: an Arabic word meaning the Father.

8.13.2.en: Out of God's tenderness, He did not make our relationship with Him that of slaves fearing the punishment of their master, but a relationship of sonship to Him. He made us call Him with the boldness of sons, saying to Him "Abba" according to the language of the Jews, or Father according to the language of the Gentiles. That is, Paul affirms sonship in his repeated calling of God Father, as if he were saying: O Papa, Father.

8.14.0.en: Heirs of God: since God is our Father, He gives us the eternal inheritance, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

8.14.1.en: Joint-heirs with Christ: Christ is the firstborn among many brethren. He entered the Kingdom as our representative, so that we also may enter on the last day and enjoy with Him His gifts in the Kingdom. We do not say "our Father" with the mouth only, but the Spirit of God within us assures us of this feeling that we are truly His beloved children, and therefore heirs of the Kingdom with His Son Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son. And if God allows us sufferings on earth, it is because He loves those who strive and endure; the Lord Christ walked first the way of sufferings and then glory, and so we also suffer first and then are glorified with an eternal glory.

8.14.2.en: God gives you, my brother, the grace of sonship and the inheritance of eternal life if you live spiritually, so how can you give up your great position and be occupied with the passing desires of the flesh?! By your spiritual conduct you are higher than the rest of the creatures, so how do you descend to animal conduct?... Let your delight be to be with God, and lift your eyes toward eternity, your natural place, and if you fall into a vile desire rise quickly, and the Holy Spirit will help you to live as a son of God.

8.15.s.en: (2) The renewal of creation and the hope of the coming glory

8.15.0.en: Who can put the limited sufferings of the present time in comparison with the glory to come that is about to be revealed in us and which we shall receive in endless eternity? The endurance of the sufferings of this age has an unlimited reward of eternal joy and happiness, and for this reason the saints longed for sufferings in order to increase their account in the coming eternal glory.

8.16.0.en: The creature: all creatures other than man, which were created for him, and were cursed because of his sin, and will be changed in eternity when man is glorified.

8.16.1.en: Eternity, in which our return to the divine embrace is completed so that we may enjoy the fullness of sonship to God, is the object of the expectation of the whole creation.

8.17.0.en: The creature was made subject to vanity, that is, the curse came upon it when Adam sinned, "cursed is the ground for thy sake" (Gen 3:17), and the phrase "not willingly" means not as a result of a fault arising from nature, but as a command of God who subjected it to destruction, yet it has a hope of being renewed and freed from the corruption and curse that came upon it, just as the children of God will be freed. But it will not be glorified, because glory belongs only to rational beings, but it will be changed to become spiritual and not material when the new heaven and the new earth appear (Rev 21:1), in which man lives forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

8.18.0.en: Creation still groans in pain to this day, since it is still a stage for wars, massacres, and famines because of man's evil, and it still travails (as if it were a womb in pain at the delivery of the child) with earthquakes, volcanoes, floods, and fires, waiting for when these painful events will end, and then nature will come to a better state suited to the revealing of man as a son of God in eternity, that is, it will be transformed, as we said, into a new heaven and a new earth.

8.19.0.en: The firstfruits of the Spirit: we have tasted the pledge of eternity in fellowship with God as a preparation for the complete fellowship in heaven.

8.19.1.en: Groan within ourselves: the sufferings that the children of God endure on earth.

8.19.2.en: Adoption: the complete sonship to God that we receive in eternity.

8.19.3.en: The redemption of our body: when bodies are changed from the material nature and dust to spiritual bodies, this we receive as grace from Christ who redeemed our spirits and our bodies.

8.19.4.en: If St. Paul, in an eloquent figure, pictured nature to us as a person who feels and senses, how much more do we human beings groan, although we have tasted some blessings of the Holy Spirit in part as a pledge of the age to come, yet we long for the whole and not the part. The fullness of sonship is not completed except after the resurrection of the bodies from death, which Christ redeemed.

8.20.0.en: The phrase "we are saved by hope" does not mean that we have already received salvation, but means that we are certain that God will fulfill for us His promise of salvation in eternal life, because God's promises are sure since He is truthful. Salvation, resurrection, and the fullness of sonship are eschatological states that take their true, open existence only in the age to come, while what we enjoy now is only a pledge of the invisible age to come. For this reason God gave us hope, by which we are confident that we shall receive eternal life, which is not seen now. Hope, beloved, is like a check in your hands now, but the date of cashing it and benefiting from it is after you leave the body, and your only weapon in cashing it is to preserve it from being lost, and to be patient until the date of cashing it at the end of your life.

8.20.1.en: If the sufferings of life are temporary, do not be troubled by them however much they multiply, but you can rise above them if you look at the heavenly glory that awaits you, and then you will receive divine help and have compassion on those who wrong you and pray for them. And although you see the sufferings with your eyes, you hardly feel them because of the abundance of God's grace supporting you.

8.21.s.en: (3) The intercession of the Holy Spirit

8.21.0.en: How are we to be patient amid the sufferings of the present and a salvation that is unseen, for the obtaining of which we pray yet do not understand its nature? In this we do not know what we should pray for, that is, the Kingdom, so the Holy Spirit intervenes to support us in our striving, give us His graces, and help us in our weakness, and not only that, but He intercedes for us and teaches us how to pray, that is, He inspires man with a prayer of the heart that the human tongue is unable to express, and gives our hearts depth in understanding and perceiving the mysteries of God that the human mind is unable to perceive. And we, as weak human beings, how do we stand before the great, holy God and speak with Him? Here the Holy Spirit intervenes and gives us the feelings with which we approach God and teaches us how to speak with Him.

8.22.0.en: The saints: God's children sanctified in Him, for everyone who believes is sanctified and set apart for Christ. The Spirit searches, that is, perceives the heart of each person individually, giving him what suits his level. The most important thing to the Spirit is the completeness of man's salvation, so He purifies our prayers of requests harmful to our salvation and answers only the requests that are according to the will of God, which certainly bring good to us.

8.22.1.en: If you do not know what to say in prayer, or the devil wars against you with laziness or wandering of thought or boredom, do not be troubled, but stand to pray and ask God's help, and He will support you and teach you everything. And what you do with difficulty now will become easy and a comfort to your heart; indeed, you will long for prayer and not want to end it, and all this by the work of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you.

8.23.0.en: God's plan for us is surpassing, for He turns all things without exception to the edification of the believer's soul, so that they work for his good on earth or for his glory in heaven. The phrase "work together" means that some individual events in our lives seem bad, harsh, and incomprehensible, but when they are added to other events, they work together in harmony, and the final picture is completed for the good and benefit of man. What seems harm now carries within it good in the future. But this privilege is only for those who love God, who, after God called them, responded to Him with love, obedience, and surrender, and lived their lives fulfilling God's purpose, that is, His will in their lives.

8.23.1.en: Note, beloved, that God's call alone does not bring about salvation, but rather the intention of those called and their obedience to God after the call. The call is not binding or compulsory, as the Lord Christ said, "For many be called, but few chosen" (Mt 20:16). So if God encourages you to a prayer, a reading, or any service, do not be lazy or put up obstacles, but hasten to respond so that you become a true son to Him.

8.24.0.en: The firstborn among many brethren: Christ, after His resurrection, ascended to heaven to declare the possibility of man's entering into the glories in the Kingdom. He is the firstborn of all who believe in Him, whom He considers brethren, that is, they will share the glory with Him in the Kingdom after they complete their spiritual striving in this life.

8.24.1.en: Whom he called: this confirms that every person who has the readiness to believe, God will call and he will receive eternal salvation. There will be no person to whom the call to life with God and to faith did not reach, except those who have no readiness for life with God, whom God knows by His foreknowledge.

8.24.2.en: God's purpose is that man should be loved as a son to Him, so He gives him a glory like the glory of His Son Jesus Christ the Firstborn. God's choosing of some and appointing them as sons to Him is not done on the basis of partiality, but on the basis of His foreknowledge of them ("whom he did foreknow") that they would respond to His call, and those who respond to the call God has justified by Baptism. So those who are steadfast in love and striving have in the end the eternal heavenly glory prepared for them before the foundation of the world.

8.25.0.en: If God is with us, that is, supports us and helps us in our weakness, then which of the wicked, or opposing factors, or adverse forces can drive us out of the circle of God's love as long as we hold fast to Him?

8.26.0.en: We cannot doubt God's love, since for our sake He gave the dearest thing He had, His only Son Jesus Christ. So it is obvious that He will give us all the gifts and graces necessary for our salvation.

8.27.0.en: If Satan accuses us of our sins before God every day, behold, Christ justifies us through our repentance.

8.28.0.en: If the wicked liars condemn us in the world with slander, as they condemned the martyrs and saints, what is the value of their condemnation when the true judgment has been placed in the hand of Christ, who died and rose and sat at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us with His blood an atoning intercession that delivers us from judgment.

8.29.s.en: (5) Nothing separates us from our love for Christ

8.29.0.en: Since God's love for us is infinite and beyond doubt, Satan's attempts are directed toward us with exhausting trials and tribulations, and their aim is to prevent us from loving God, and Satan often succeeds in that. But St. Paul cries out with confidence together with the elect who are steadfast in their love for God, saying that nothing separates us from God, whether tribulation, which is pressure and injustice, or distress, which is more violent than tribulation, persecution, that is, inflicting harm and crushing, and famine, which is the cutting off of all the resources of life, and nakedness, that is, lack of necessary clothing, then peril and sword, that is, the threat to the Christian's life even unto death.

8.30.0.en: History bears witness to the multitude of martyrs who are killed all the day long, that is, throughout the days, like sheep, because of their love for the King Christ. And every Christian accepts death throughout his life in enduring sufferings, whether in the struggle against sin, or asceticism, or self-giving service, and even more in the torments of martyrdom for the love of Christ.

8.31.0.en: Thus we win a great victory over Satan and his helpers, and enter into eternal glory, after Satan has exhausted all his tricks of tribulations and death in the hope of turning us away from our love for Christ; indeed, we are more than conquerors through the very things that were set for our snares, and if we are struck we are counted stronger than those who strike, because God wrestles with us.

8.32.0.en: St. Paul returns to affirm that our love for Christ, who loved us first, cannot be weakened by fear of death or love of life. As for his mention of the angels and some of their orders (principalities and powers), what is meant is that we love Christ not for the sake of our future enjoyment of the presence of the angels, but for the sake of His beloved Person.

8.32.1.en: The Paradise of the Fathers tells us that a monk saw a real angel while he was praying, and he continued in his prayer without paying attention to the angel.

8.32.2.en: Nor can the enticements of the world in the present and the future, which rise and fall in many fluctuations, or any other creature, whatever it may be, separate us from our love for Christ; the goal of our life is to love Him and to enjoy His love for us, and welcome to death if it shortens our way to meet our heavenly Bridegroom.

8.32.3.en: Examine yourself at the end of each day: what hindered you from enjoying the love of Christ, and however dear it is, do not let it deprive you of the goal of your life.

8.32.4.en: Make more room of time and give up, not only evil desires or the worries and disturbances of life, but any occupation that deprives you of your spiritual life.
